content: Hoechst AG was a German life sciences company that played a significant role in the global pharmaceutical market. It was often referred to as The pharmacy of the world due to its substantial contributions to the drug industry. The company was originally established in 1863 under the name Teerfarbenfabrik Meister, Lucius & Co. in Höchst, near Frankfurt. A few years later, it was renamed Teerfarbenfabrik Meister Lucius & Brüning. By 1880, it had transitioned into a stock company under the name Farbwerke vorm Meister Lucius & Brüning AG. For international branding purposes, the name was later simplified to Farbwerke Hoechst AG. Until 1925, Hoechst AG operated as an independent entity. In 1916, Hoechst AG became one of the founding members of IG Farben, a coalition of German chemical companies formed to consolidate industrial power during World War I and its aftermath. However, following its dissolution in 1951, Hoechst AG was re-established on December 7, 1951, in Frankfurt, with an initial capitalization of 100,000 Deutsche Marks. In 1987, Hoechst acquired the American chemical company Celanese, leading to the creation of a U.S. subsidiary named Hoechst Celanese. In 1994, the U.S. National Right to Life Committee initiated a boycott of all Hoechst pharmaceutical products, including Altace, due to ethical concerns. On September 17, 1994, Pharmacists For Life International joined the boycott, targeting Hoechst's American subsidiaries, including Hoechst-Roussel, Hoechst-Celanese, and Copley Pharmaceuticals, as well as its agricultural division. The group encouraged consumers to focus on boycotting key Hoechst drugs, such as Altace, to maximize economic impact. In 1995, Hoechst merged with Marion Merrill Dow, a Kansas City-based company, forming a U.S. subsidiary called Hoechst Marion Roussel (HMR). During this time, Altace generated less than $90 million in revenue for Hoechst, and the company ceased promoting the drug in the U.S. That same year, Jefferson Jeff Gregory, President of King Pharmaceuticals, began negotiations with Hoechst to acquire U.S. distribution rights for Altace. In 1997, Hoechst underwent a corporate restructuring, transferring its various business units to independent companies, including Nutrinova and Clariant. On April 2, 1997, the anti-abortion group Concerned Women for America announced at a National Right to Life Committee press briefing that the boycott against Hoechst AG and its subsidiaries would be more narrowly focused on specific HMR prescription drugs, such as Allegra, Cardizem, Seldane, Claforan, Lasix, DiaBeta, and Nicoderm. Notably, Altace was no longer included in the boycott list. On December 18, 1998, King Pharmaceuticals, through its wholly owned subsidiary Monarch Pharmaceuticals, Inc., acquired the U.S. distribution rights to Altace and other Hoechst products from Hoechst Marion Roussel. In 1999, Hoechst AG merged with Rhône-Poulenc S.A. to form Aventis, a new company headquartered in Strasbourg, France. As part of the merger, Hoechst divested many of its industrial businesses, including Celanese, which became an independent company once again. On December 7, 1999, Hoechst and Rhône-Poulenc resolved charges from the Federal Trade Commission, which had alleged that their merger would violate U.S. antitrust laws.
